analysis_notes.notes:
Torah LM2/50 is a very short teaching (three brief paragraphs) on the control of thought. The dataset contains zero entries with reference=1050, confirmed by scanning the full torahData.js file — the dataset jumps directly from reference 1049 to 1051. Therefore no bechina subgraph can be constructed and no packages can be formed.

The teaching's content: (1) Thought (מַחֲשָׁבָה) is in the person's hand to direct wherever they wish — it is impossible for two thoughts to coexist simultaneously. (2) Even when thought wanders and flutters toward alien/foreign matters (דְּבָרִים אֲחֵרִים וְזָרִים), one can forcibly return it to the straight path (הַדֶּרֶךְ הַיָּשָׁר). (3) This is analogous to a horse (סוּס) straying from the road — you grab it with a halter (אַפְסָר) and force it back; so too with thought.

Bechina language scan: The source text contains no explicit bechina markers. There is no occurrence of 'בְּחִינַת', 'הוא בְּחִינַת', or 'נִקְרָא' linking two concepts in an identity statement. The horse analogy is a mashal (illustrative parable) — it maps thought to a horse functionally (both can stray, both can be forcibly redirected), but this is an analogy within the argument, not an ontological identity equation of the bechina type. The Rebbe uses the phrase 'כְּמוֹ סוּס' (like a horse) and 'כְּמוֹ־כֵן' (similarly), the language of comparison, not the language of bechina identity.

Conclusion: Torah LM2/50 operates entirely on the practical and descriptive axis. There are no bechina pairs present in the source text and none in the dataset. No additions are proposed.
